---
title: "Wrangling data"
subtitle: "Shape a dataset for `#plot`: coerce, summarise, reshape, and join a row-store with native Typst and the wrangle verbs."
engine: markdown
---

Gribouille reads a dataset as a _row-store_: an array of dictionaries, one dictionary per row, with the column names as shared keys.
That is exactly the shape `csv("file.csv", row-type: dictionary)` returns, and the shape `#plot` expects.
Because a row-store is an ordinary Typst array, most preparation is just array methods you already have.
The wrangle verbs fill the three gaps native Typst leaves open: grouped aggregation, reshaping, and joining.
Every wrangle verb accepts a row-store (or a column-store dictionary of arrays) and returns a row-store, so its result feeds `#plot` with no adapter.

::: {.callout-note}
The wrangle verbs are experimental: their interfaces may change without notice while the design settles, and they may move into a dedicated Typst data-wrangling package in the future.
Native Typst array methods and the plotting API remain stable.
:::

Each example below uses only the bundled datasets ([`mpg`](../reference/datasets/mpg.qmd), [`penguins`](../reference/datasets/penguins.qmd)).

## Native Typst or a verb?

Reach for a wrangle verb only when native Typst has no clean equivalent.
Rowwise work is already a one-liner, so wrapping it would add a name without adding power.

| Task                              | Use                                                                                                            |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Keep rows matching a condition    | `data.filter(row => row.hwy > 30)`                                                                             |
| Derive or rewrite a column        | `data.map(row => (..row, ratio: row.hwy / row.cty))`                                                           |
| Sort rows                         | `data.sorted(key: row => row.hwy)` (append `.rev()` to descend)                                                |
| First or last few rows            | `data.slice(0, 5)`                                                                                             |
| Drop exact duplicate rows         | `data.dedup()`                                                                                                 |
| **Aggregate rows per group**      | [`summarise`](../reference/helpers/summarise.qmd), [`count`](../reference/helpers/count.qmd)                   |
| **Reshape long or wide**          | [`pivot-longer`](../reference/helpers/pivot-longer.qmd), [`pivot-wider`](../reference/helpers/pivot-wider.qmd) |
| **Combine two datasets on a key** | [`left-join`](../reference/helpers/left-join.qmd) and friends                                                  |

The verbs that _do_ exist for column work ([`select`](../reference/helpers/select.qmd), [`rename`](../reference/helpers/rename.qmd), [`relocate`](../reference/helpers/relocate.qmd), [`drop-na`](../reference/helpers/drop-na.qmd), [`distinct`](../reference/helpers/distinct.qmd), [`slice-max`](../reference/helpers/slice-max.qmd)) earn their place by naming a fiddly pattern: keyed de-duplication, per-group top-n, or missing-value handling that a bare `.filter` states awkwardly.

## Coerce columns

A dataset read from a CSV arrives as strings, and real files spell missing values in several ways.
[`as-numeric`](../reference/core/as-numeric.qmd) parses a column to numbers in one pass, and its `na:` argument blanks the placeholders so they do not survive as spurious values.

```typst
// A row-store as csv(..., row-type: dictionary) would return it.
#let raw = (
  (class: "compact", hwy: "29"),
  (class: "midsize", hwy: "NA"),
  (class: "suv", hwy: "18"),
)

#let clean = as-numeric(raw, "hwy", na: ("NA",))
// clean == ((class: "compact", hwy: 29.0),
//           (class: "midsize", hwy: none),
//           (class: "suv", hwy: 18.0))
```

Pair it with [`drop-na`](../reference/helpers/drop-na.qmd) to remove the rows that became `none`, then plot.
The bundled `mpg` is already typed, so the sections below skip this step.

## Summarise by group

[`summarise`](../reference/helpers/summarise.qmd) collapses each group to a single row.
Grouping is per-call through `by:`; there is no persistent grouped state to remember to undo.
Each aggregation is a closure that receives the group's rows and returns one cell, so any expression over the rows is fair game, including counts and multi-column ratios that a column-at-a-time helper could not express.

```{typst}
//| echo: true
//| output-filename: "wrangle-summarise.svg"
//| alt: "Bar chart of mean highway fuel economy by vehicle class, sorted ascending from pickup and SUV at the low end to compact and subcompact at the high end; each class is a single bar."
#let by-class = summarise(
  mpg,
  mean-hwy: rows => rows.map(row => row.hwy).sum() / rows.len(),
  n: rows => rows.len(),
  by: "class",
).sorted(key: row => row.mean-hwy)

#plot(
  data: by-class,
  mapping: aes(x: "class", y: "mean-hwy"),
  layers: (geom-col(fill: okabe-ito.at(4)),),
  scales: scales(x: scale-discrete(limits: by-class.map(row => row.class))),
  labels: labels(
    title: "Fuel economy by vehicle class",
    x: "Vehicle class",
    y: "Mean highway mpg",
  ),
  width: 12cm,
  height: 7cm,
)
```

When the aggregation is just a tally, [`count`](../reference/helpers/count.qmd) is the shorthand: it groups by the columns you name and adds an `n` column, and `sort: true` orders the groups from most to least frequent.

```{typst}
//| echo: true
//| output-filename: "wrangle-count.svg"
//| alt: "Horizontal-reading bar chart of the number of vehicles in each class, ordered from the most common class down to the least, with SUV the tallest bar."
#let counts = count(mpg, "class", sort: true)

#plot(
  data: counts,
  mapping: aes(x: "class", y: "n"),
  layers: (geom-col(fill: okabe-ito.at(2)),),
  scales: scales(x: scale-discrete(limits: counts.map(row => row.class))),
  labels: labels(title: "Vehicles per class", x: "Vehicle class", y: "Count"),
  width: 12cm,
  height: 7cm,
)
```

## Reshape long or wide

Two columns that measure the same thing, such as city and highway economy, are often easier to plot once melted into a single value column with a label column beside it.
[`pivot-longer`](../reference/helpers/pivot-longer.qmd) gathers the named columns into a `names-to`/`values-to` pair, carrying the other columns through, so one mapping can colour or facet by the measurement.

```{typst}
//| echo: true
//| output-filename: "wrangle-pivot.svg"
//| alt: "Two side-by-side box plots of miles per gallon, one for city and one for highway economy; the highway box sits noticeably higher than the city box, both drawn from the same vehicles."
#let long = pivot-longer(
  mpg,
  ("cty", "hwy"),
  names-to: "metric",
  values-to: "mpg",
)

#plot(
  data: long,
  mapping: aes(x: "metric", y: "mpg", fill: "metric"),
  layers: (geom-boxplot(),),
  labels: labels(title: "City versus highway economy", x: "Metric", y: "Miles per gallon"),
  width: 10cm,
  height: 7cm,
)
```

[`pivot-wider`](../reference/helpers/pivot-wider.qmd) is the inverse: it spreads a label column back into one column per level, round-tripping the reshape when you need a wide table again.

## Join a lookup

Enriching a dataset with a lookup table is a join, not a manual `dict.at(key)` per row.
Build the lookup as its own small row-store and [`left-join`](../reference/helpers/left-join.qmd) it on the shared key: every row of the left dataset is kept, gaining the lookup's extra columns.

```{typst}
//| echo: true
//| output-filename: "wrangle-join.svg"
//| alt: "Bar chart of mean highway economy by vehicle class, sorted ascending, with bars coloured by a joined vehicle kind: cars in one colour, SUV, van, and truck classes in others, showing the efficient classes are cars."
#let by-class = summarise(
  mpg,
  mean-hwy: rows => rows.map(row => row.hwy).sum() / rows.len(),
  by: "class",
).sorted(key: row => row.mean-hwy)

#let kind = (
  (class: "compact", kind: "Car"),
  (class: "subcompact", kind: "Car"),
  (class: "midsize", kind: "Car"),
  (class: "2seater", kind: "Car"),
  (class: "minivan", kind: "Van"),
  (class: "suv", kind: "SUV"),
  (class: "pickup", kind: "Truck"),
)

#let enriched = left-join(by-class, kind, by: "class")

#plot(
  data: enriched,
  mapping: aes(x: "class", y: "mean-hwy", fill: "kind"),
  layers: (geom-col(),),
  scales: scales(x: scale-discrete(limits: enriched.map(row => row.class))),
  labels: labels(title: "Economy by class and kind", x: "Vehicle class", y: "Mean highway mpg", fill: "Kind"),
  width: 12cm,
  height: 7cm,
)
```

The other joins share the `by:` interface: [`inner-join`](../reference/helpers/inner-join.qmd) keeps only matched rows, [`full-join`](../reference/helpers/full-join.qmd) keeps both sides, and [`semi-join`](../reference/helpers/semi-join.qmd)/[`anti-join`](../reference/helpers/anti-join.qmd) filter the left dataset by whether a key exists in the right without adding columns.
To stack datasets that share columns instead of matching on a key, [`bind-rows`](../reference/helpers/bind-rows.qmd) unions their rows and fills any missing columns with `none`.

## Putting it together

A whole preparation reads as one expression: summarise, enrich, then hand the result straight to `#plot`.
With a real CSV you would open with `as-numeric` to type the measured columns first.

```typst
#let data = left-join(
  summarise(
    mpg,
    mean-hwy: rows => rows.map(row => row.hwy).sum() / rows.len(),
    by: "class",
  ),
  kind,
  by: "class",
)

#plot(data: data, mapping: aes(x: "class", y: "mean-hwy", fill: "kind"), ...)
```

- [`as-numeric`](../reference/core/as-numeric.qmd) and [`as-factor`](../reference/core/as-factor.qmd) coerce a column to numbers or to a discrete factor.
